summary: For ages 9–11 (Endangered & Extinct Species): establish precisely that endangered means a species is at high risk but still surviving, while extinct means none remain anywhere. Pupils diagnose WHY specific species decline — habitat destruction (usually the leading driver), hunting/poaching, pollution, climate change, invasive species — using evidence (population trend, range, threats) rather than memorising a list, and learn the IUCN Red List as an evidence-based scientific ranking of extinction risk, not an opinion.
misconceptions: 'Endangered and extinct mean the same thing' — endangered = at high risk but still alive; extinct = none remain.
'Extinction is always caused by humans' — extinction also occurs naturally, though current rates are greatly raised by human activity.
'Extinct animals can be brought back easily' — extinction is (currently) permanent; there is no simple undo.
'If a few individuals survive, the species is safe' — very small populations can still be doomed (low genetic diversity, unable to recover).
'The Red List is just an opinion / a list of favourites' — it is an evidence-based scientific classification of extinction risk.

activities.title: Species case-file: become a Red List assessor
steps: Open a 'file' for a real species (e.g. giant panda, mountain gorilla, Amur leopard) containing a population graph over time, the size of its range, and the threats it faces.

Decide where the species belongs on the risk ladder (Least Concern → Near Threatened → Vulnerable → Endangered → Critically Endangered → Extinct in the Wild → Extinct) and justify the placement from the evidence shown.
Compare your placement with the species' actual, current Red List classification and state what evidence drove the real decision.

For each species, write one sentence naming the main threat and how it drives the decline (e.g. 'deforestation removes the orangutan's food and shelter, so its numbers can fall even without any hunting').
activities.insight: Endangered and extinct are different points on one evidence-based scale, and a species' position is a measured judgement from population size, range and rate of decline — not a label or a favourite.

activities.title: Live pressure: watch a species slide down the ladder
steps: Starting from a stable population, increase a single pressure (e.g. habitat loss, or poaching) a little at a time.
Watch the population curve bend downward and note at what point the species crosses from one risk category into the next.
Describe in words what happened: which pressure you changed, and how far along the ladder it pushed the species.
Repeat with a different pressure to compare how different threats drive decline.
activities.insight: Specific human pressures push a species along the risk scale; 'endangered' becomes a measured position driven by evidence, and conservation can be pictured as pushing species back up the ladder.

activities.title: Cause diagnosis: why is THIS animal at risk?
steps: For several declining species, match each to the threat(s) actually driving its decline (habitat loss → orangutan/deforestation; poaching → rhino horn/elephant ivory; climate change → polar bear/coral; invasive species → island birds; pollution → species harmed by chemicals or plastics in their habitat).
For at least one species, explain how an indirect cause (habitat loss) harms the animal even when no one is hunting it — what food, shelter or breeding space is lost.
Sort example species into 'endangered (still alive, at risk)' versus 'extinct (none left)', placing panda and mountain gorilla as endangered and dodo and thylacine as extinct.
activities.insight: Different animals are endangered for different, identifiable reasons; habitat destruction is usually the leading driver even without direct killing; and endangered is firmly distinct from extinct.

activities.title: Shrinking-habitat investigation (physical, no screen needed)
steps: Mark out a large area as a 'habitat' and have pupils stand as 'animals', each needing personal space to survive.
Predict how many animals can survive, then repeatedly halve the habitat area and record how many must leave each time.
Discuss: no one was 'hunting' — so why did the population crash? Connect this to real deforestation, wetland draining and reef damage.

Respond to prompts: Could a rainforest monkey become endangered if no one hunted it? What is the difference between endangered and extinct? Why can't we always bring an extinct animal back? What is the IUCN Red List for?
activities.insight: Habitat loss alone, with no hunting, can drive a species toward extinction — making the leading, indirect cause tangible.

activities.title: In role: how an assessor decides a category (optional hook)
steps: Read or listen to a short explanation, in the voice of a conservation scientist, of how a Red List category is chosen from evidence.
Note which pieces of evidence the assessor says they weigh (population size, range, rate of decline).
Then return to a case-file and apply the same reasoning to justify a category yourself.
activities.insight: Red List categories come from stated evidence and criteria, so classification is reasoned, not arbitrary.

checkQuestion: More species are becoming endangered today than ever before. A student says the main reason is that hunters are shooting too many animals. Is hunting really the biggest cause — or is something else driving most species toward extinction?
checkAnswer: Hunting and poaching matter, but for most species the biggest cause is habitat destruction — when forests are cleared, wetlands drained or reefs damaged, animals lose the places they need to feed, shelter and breed, so whole populations decline even when no one hunts them. Pollution, climate change and invasive species add to this. So the main driver is usually loss of habitat, not shooting.
